reels.title: Many kitchens, not one cook

beats.say: Imagine one chef chopping a thousand onions. Hiring a second chef in the same tiny kitchen doesn't help, if they must share one knife. So what does?
Give each chef their own kitchen, their own knife, their own board. Now four chefs chop four piles at once. In Python, each kitchen is a process, and it can use its own processor core.

chip.text: All cores work at the same time

beats.say: But there is a price. Opening a kitchen takes time, and passing ingredients between kitchens means packing them in boxes and copying them. So send a short order, like a pile number, and get back a small note, like the onion count.

chip.text: Copying big boxes erases the gain

check.q: In the kitchen picture, what is the best thing to hand each separate kitchen?
opts: A short note saying which pile to chop
A copy of every other kitchen's results
check.why: Passing data between processes means copying it, so small inputs and small results keep the copying cost low and the parallel gain intact.

work: Think of one slow job at work that is pure calculation and could be split into independent piles.
Write down what each worker would receive and return, and check both are small.

reels.title: Eight cores, eight locks

beats.say: You have eight cores and eight hundred files, each taking two seconds of pure CPU. Why do threads take about twenty-six minutes, while processes take about three?
Each process has its own interpreter and its own GIL, the lock that lets only one thread run Python code at a time. Eight processes means eight locks, so eight cores work at once.
ProcessPoolExecutor starts one worker per core by default. Pool dot map sends each file path to a worker, which parses it and returns counts. Then you merge the counts.
Arguments and results are pickled, meaning turned into bytes and copied across. So pass paths, and return summaries.

show.title: Keep the traffic small
items: Pickled means turned into bytes and copied
Send a path, not the file contents

check.q: Why can eight processes beat eight threads on pure Python number crunching?
opts: Processes get faster memory than threads
Each process has its own GIL and its own core
Threads can only work on one file at a time
check.why: Threads in one process share a single GIL, so only one runs Python code at a time. Separate processes each have their own interpreter and GIL.

work: Benchmark your CPU-heavy loop with one worker, then with a process pool, and compare real timings.
Change the worker function to take a file path and return a small summary.

reels.title: Why your pool hangs on a Mac

beats.say: Your pool code works on Linux, then hangs or crashes on a Mac. Why?

show.text: Works on Linux. Breaks on macOS.

beats.say: On macOS and Windows, workers start by spawn. A fresh interpreter imports your script from the top. Without the main guard, each worker would try to start more workers, and everything blows up. So wrap the launch in if name equals main.

show.title: The main guard

beats.say: Functions must be top level, because pickle sends them by name. A lambda or nested function fails to pickle, and you get an error.
And watch size. Sending a two gigabyte DataFrame to each of eight workers copies sixteen gigabytes, and erases the gain. Startup also costs around a tenth of a second per worker, so tiny tasks lose.

check.q: Your pool task takes five milliseconds and you submit a million of them one by one. What is the likely result?
opts: Slower than a plain loop, because pickling and messaging dominate
It fails because of the GIL
check.why: Each task pays for pickling and inter-process messaging. When the work per task is tiny, that overhead exceeds the work. Batch tasks into larger chunks.

work: Add the main guard to every script that creates a process pool, and test it on macOS or Windows.
Give each task enough work, such as a whole file or a range of rows, to outweigh the copy cost.

reels.title: When a process pool is not the answer

beats.say: When should you not reach for a process pool?
It stops at one machine. Eight cores gives at best eight times faster, and memory is multiplied by the worker count. Past that, you need a cluster.

The shape you wrote, split, process, merge small results, is MapReduce. Spark executors work the same way: each task handles one partition and returns a partial result. So the design scales out when data outgrows one box.

But first, measure. If time goes to waiting on networks, use threads or asyncio. If NumPy or the database does the work in native code, you may need no processes. Choose processes for proven Python CPU work with small inputs and outputs.

show.title: Choose by bottleneck
items: Waiting on network: threads or asyncio
Native vectorised code: often no pool needed
Python CPU work, small data: processes
Beyond one machine: Spark or similar

check.q: A job is slow because it waits on thousands of API calls. What should you choose?
opts: A process pool with one worker per core
Threads or asyncio, since the wait is not CPU
Pickle the responses to speed things up
check.why: Waiting on I/O releases the GIL and uses no CPU, so threads or asyncio overlap the waits cheaply. Processes add copying and memory cost for no benefit.

work: Profile a slow job and label it CPU-bound, I/O-bound or native-code-bound before picking a tool.
Note the point where one machine's cores or memory run out, and what you would move to next.

reels.title: The buzzer and the kitchen

beats.say: Ever ordered at a food court and been handed a buzzer?
The buzzer is a promise of food later. Meanwhile you are free to do other things. In Python, that promise is called a future.
The kitchen has a fixed number of cooks. That is the pool. Extra orders wait in line, so the kitchen is never swamped.
When a buzzer goes off, you collect that meal. If the cook burned it, you only find out at pickup. And you can swap cooks sharing one kitchen for separate kitchens, without changing how you order.

show.title: Same way to order
items: Buzzer goes off: collect the meal
Burned meal: you learn at pickup

check.q: In the food court analogy, what does a future correspond to?
opts: The buzzer, a promise of a result later
check.why: A future is a placeholder you hold while the work happens elsewhere. It later holds a result or an error, just like a buzzer leads to your meal.

work: Spot one place in your code where you wait for slow calls one after another.
Say out loud what the future, the pool and the result are in that code.

reels.title: Submit, futures and as_completed

beats.say: You have one hundred URLs to fetch. How do you finish in seconds, not minutes?
Each fetch waits about half a second on the network. One after another, that is fifty seconds. A pool of eight threads overlaps the waiting, so it takes about six seconds.
Calling submit returns a future at once. It is a placeholder that later holds a result or an error. Calling result on it waits if needed, and re-raises any worker exception.
Map gives results in input order. As completed gives them the moment each finishes, so one slow URL never blocks the rest.

show.title: Pick your order
items: map: input order, first error on reach
submit plus as_completed: first done, first handled
Per-item try and except only with submit

check.q: You want to log each failed URL and keep going while others finish. What fits best?
opts: pool.map and one try around the loop
submit with as_completed and try around each result call
A single thread in a for loop
check.why: With submit and as_completed you handle each future when it finishes, and a try around result lets one failure be logged without stopping the others.

work: Time a sequential fetch loop, then the same with eight workers, and compare.
Replace a map call that hides failures with submit and as_completed plus per-item logging.

reels.title: Silent errors and hung pools

beats.say: Your worker threw an error, so why did your program stay silent?
With submit, the exception is stored inside the future. It only surfaces when you call result. If you never call it, the failure vanishes. Always wrap result in a try block.

Map is different. It raises the first error when you reach that item in order, and the remaining results are lost to your loop. Also, leaving the with block waits for every pending job, so a hung task hangs your program. Set timeouts.

show.title: Map and the with block
items: map raises at the failing item, in order
Later results are lost to your loop
Leaving with waits for all pending jobs
A hung task hangs the program: set timeouts

beats.say: Threads cannot stop a running job. Cancel only works on jobs still waiting in the queue. And processes need arguments and results that can be pickled, meaning turned into bytes, which costs time.

show.title: Limits
items: Cancel works only on queued jobs
Process pools need picklable inputs and outputs

check.q: You submit 50 jobs and never call result on the futures. One job raises an error. What happens?
opts: The error is stored in the future and goes unnoticed
The pool retries the job automatically
check.why: The exception lives inside the future until result or exception is called. Ignoring the futures means silent failure.

work: Audit every submit call and confirm each future has result called inside a try block.
Add a timeout to result calls and to any network call inside workers.

reels.title: When a pool is the wrong tool

beats.say: Is a thread pool the right tool for ten thousand calls?
Probably not. Each thread costs memory, so pools stay in the tens. For thousands of network calls, asyncio handles them on one thread with far less overhead.
For CPU work, swap in a process pool. But pickling and startup cost mean tiny tasks get slower. Batch work into chunks, and size workers to your core count.

show.title: CPU-bound work
items: Pickling and startup hurt tiny tasks

beats.say: Also respect the other side. Eight workers hitting one API can trigger rate limits, so pool size is a throttle. For retries, queues, and scheduling across machines, choose a task queue or Spark instead. One pool is for one machine.

check.q: You must make 20,000 small HTTP calls and later scale across several machines with retries. What is the best choice?
opts: asyncio for the calls, and a task queue or distributed framework to spread them
check.why: Asyncio handles huge counts of waiting I/O cheaply, and an executor cannot span machines or provide retries, so a queue or distributed framework fits the scale-out need.

work: Write down the rate limit of each API you call and set pool size below it.
Benchmark a process pool with chunked batches against per-item tasks before adopting it.

reels.title: Waiting versus working, in a kitchen

beats.say: Why can't ten extra cooks make water boil faster?

Because boiling is waiting. While the pot heats, one smart cook chops onions. That is concurrency: juggling jobs while one of them waits. Programs wait too, on web calls, database answers and file downloads.
Chopping is different. The cook is busy every second, so juggling does not help. You need more hands working at the same instant. That is parallelism. In a computer, those hands are processor cores.
So before picking a tool, ask one question. Is my program mostly waiting, or mostly working? Waiting calls for juggling. Working calls for more cores.

check.q: A program spends most of its time waiting for web replies. What helps most?
opts: Buying a CPU with more cores
Rewriting the loop to be shorter
check.why: The processor is idle during waiting, so overlapping the waits gains the most. More cores would sit idle too.

work: For a slow job at work, say out loud whether it is waiting or computing before touching code.
List three jobs in your pipelines that mostly wait on APIs, databases or storage.

reels.title: Concurrency or parallelism: the numbers

beats.say: A crawler makes one hundred API calls, each taking two hundred milliseconds. How long does it take?

One after another, twenty seconds. But the program only computes for about one millisecond per call. The rest is waiting on the network. With twenty calls in flight at once, using threads or asyncio, the same job finishes in about one second.

Now flip it. Eight files, each needing ten seconds of pure parsing. The core is never idle, so interleaving gains nothing. Eight processes on eight cores finish in about ten seconds instead of eighty.
Best of all, use an engine that is already parallel, like DuckDB, Polars or Spark. Then you write no concurrency code at all.

show.title: Prefer a parallel engine
items: DuckDB and Polars use all local cores
No threads or locks in your code

check.q: Eight files each need ten seconds of pure CPU parsing, and you have eight cores. Which approach gets close to ten seconds in total?
opts: One thread per file in plain Python
check.why: Pure computing keeps a core busy, so overlapping does not help. Separate processes use separate cores at the same instant.

work: Time one slow step with a stopwatch, then compare time spent waiting against time spent computing.
Before writing a worker pool, check whether DuckDB or Polars can do the transformation directly.

reels.title: Where threads, processes and asyncio bite

beats.say: Why can ten Python threads run a pure loop no faster than one?

The global interpreter lock lets only one thread run Python code at a time. Threads still help with waiting, because a thread releases the lock while it waits on the network. For computing, it just adds switching overhead. Use processes, each with its own lock.

Processes have costs too. Data sent between them is copied, so shipping big objects can cost more than the work saved. Asyncio has its own trap: one blocking call, like a slow library read, freezes every other task, because they share one thread.

show.title: Hidden costs
items: Processes: data is copied between them
Processes: extra memory and startup time
Asyncio: one blocking call freezes all tasks

beats.say: And more concurrency is not always better. Fire a thousand requests at once and the server answers with rate limit errors. Cap the number in flight, and retry with backoff.

check.q: An asyncio crawler stalls completely whenever one task parses a large file with a normal blocking function. Why?
opts: Asyncio tasks each use their own process
The blocking call holds the single thread running every task
check.why: Asyncio runs all tasks on one thread, so a call that never yields stops the event loop until it finishes.

work: Add a semaphore or pool size limit to any crawler that has no cap on requests in flight.
Search async code for blocking calls and move heavy ones to a process pool.

reels.title: When not to write concurrency code

beats.say: When is writing concurrency code the wrong answer?

Often. First measure. Profile where the time goes. If a query spends ninety percent of its time in one slow database scan, threads change nothing; an index or a better plan does. Concurrency adds bugs, hard debugging and memory cost.

For heavy transformation, prefer a parallel engine. DuckDB or Polars use every core on one machine. Spark spreads work across machines when data outgrows one box. Each worker you add also costs money, so scale only past the measured limit.

steps.label: Cluster: Spark, when data outgrows a box

beats.say: Keep concurrency for waiting work: crawlers, fan out API calls, object store reads. Use asyncio for thousands of connections, threads for a few dozen with simple blocking libraries. Bound both by the other system's limits.

show.title: Where concurrency fits
items: Waiting work: crawlers, API fan out, storage reads
Threads: a few dozen, blocking libraries
Always cap by the other side's limits

check.q: A nightly job joins and aggregates 40 GB of Parquet on one large machine and is slow. What is the best first move?
opts: Wrap the Python loop in a thread pool
Measure, then use a parallel engine such as DuckDB or Polars
Move straight to a Spark cluster
check.why: The work is computing, so threads will not help. A parallel engine uses all cores with no concurrency code, and a cluster is justified only after measuring a real limit.

work: Make profiling output a required step before approving any concurrency pull request.
Write down the limits of your busiest upstream API so every crawler uses a matching cap.

reels.title: One waiter, twenty tables

beats.say: How can one waiter serve twenty tables at the same time?
He takes an order, hands it to the kitchen, and does not stand there waiting. He walks to the next table. When the kitchen rings the bell, he comes back and delivers the food.
That waiter is asyncio. The tables are tasks. The bell is the moment a slow answer arrives. One person, many jobs, because most of the time is spent waiting.

show.title: The mapping
items: Waiting, not working, is the big cost

beats.say: But if the waiter stops to cook a dish himself, every table sits hungry. Slow work that blocks is the danger.

show.sub: The waiter cannot cook and serve

check.q: In the waiter analogy, why can one waiter serve many tables?
opts: He works much faster than normal
He moves on while the kitchen is slow
check.why: Most of the time is spent waiting on the kitchen. Using that wait to serve other tables is what asyncio does.

work: List the slow waiting steps in one of your jobs, such as API calls or database reads.
Ask whether each waiting step could run while others wait.

reels.title: Ten thousand calls in four minutes

beats.say: Ten thousand API calls, each taking half a second. How long if you make them one by one?

show.sub: 10,000 calls x 0.5 s, one at a time

beats.say: About eighty three minutes. With asyncio, a coroutine runs until it reaches await on something slow, like a network call. Then it hands control back to the event loop, which starts another task.
A semaphore caps how many are in flight, say twenty. With twenty at a time, ten thousand calls at half a second each take about four minutes.
Gather collects the results in input order. All of it runs on one thread, switching only at await.

show.title: Pattern
show.text:
sem = asyncio.Semaphore(20)
async with sem:
    await fetch(client, i)
await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

check.q: With a semaphore of 20 and 0.5 second calls, roughly how long do 10,000 calls take?
check.why: 10,000 divided by 20 is 500 rounds of 0.5 seconds, about 250 seconds.

work: Time a sequential batch of calls, then the same batch with a semaphore.
Pick a limit from the API's documented rate limit, not a guess.

reels.title: The one line that freezes everything

beats.say: Why can one line of code freeze two hundred running tasks?

show.text: One blocking call = all tasks stop

beats.say: Because asyncio switches tasks only at await. Call time dot sleep or requests dot get, and the thread is stuck. The event loop cannot run anything else until it returns.
Fix it by using async libraries like httpx, asyncpg, or aiobotocore. For blocking code you cannot replace, use asyncio dot to thread, which runs it on a worker thread.
Also, gather without a semaphore launches all ten thousand at once, and you hit rate limits or run out of sockets. And heavy CPU work blocks the loop too, since it never awaits.

show.title: Other traps
items: No semaphore: rate limits, socket exhaustion
gather returns results in input order

check.q: A coroutine calls requests.get inside an async function. What happens?
opts: Every task on the loop stalls until it returns
check.why: requests.get never awaits, so the single thread never returns to the event loop.

work: Search your async code for requests, time.sleep and sync database drivers.
Wrap unavoidable blocking calls in asyncio.to_thread.
Always bound concurrency with a semaphore.

reels.title: When asyncio is the wrong tool

beats.say: When is asyncio the wrong choice?
It shines for many waiting calls: thousands of requests, small memory, no thread per call. Match the semaphore to the downstream rate limit, such as an agent running five hundred LLM test cases.
It does nothing for CPU heavy work. Use processes there. If your libraries are only blocking, threads are simpler than rewriting everything.
The cost is async spreading through the codebase, harder debugging, and one blocking call hurting everyone. Measure first: if the job is not wait-bound, asyncio buys nothing.

show.title: Costs
items: One blocking call hurts all tasks

check.q: A job is slow because it parses large files with heavy computation. What fits best?
check.why: CPU-bound work needs real parallelism. asyncio only overlaps waiting on one thread.

work: Profile first to see whether time goes to waiting or computing.
Set concurrency from the downstream rate limit and measure the result.
Use threads when only sync libraries exist and scale is modest.

reels.title: The kitchen with too many orders

beats.say: What happens when a thousand customers shout orders at one tiny kitchen at the same time?

The kitchen collapses. Orders pile up, cooks panic, and everyone waits longer. A computer service does the same when too many requests arrive at once. It starts refusing them, with an error called four twenty nine, which means too many requests.

Two simple rules fix it. First, a limit on how many orders the cooks handle at once, say three. That is a semaphore, a counter of free seats. Second, a ticket machine that hands out one ticket per second. No ticket, you wait.
And if the kitchen is slow, the waiter stops taking new orders instead of stacking paper slips on the counter. That is backpressure.

check.q: In the kitchen story, what does backpressure mean?
opts: Cooks work faster when orders pile up
The waiter stops taking new orders while the kitchen is busy
check.why: Backpressure makes the faster upstream side slow down to match the slower downstream side, instead of letting work pile up.

work: List the outside services your code calls and write down each one's documented rate limit.
Find one place where your code fires requests as fast as it can, and note what would happen at ten times the load.

reels.title: Token bucket and semaphore

beats.say: How can a limiter allow a burst of three calls, yet still average only one call per second?

show.text: Burst of 3, average of 1 per second

beats.say: It uses a token bucket. The bucket holds at most capacity tokens, here three. Tokens drip in at rate one per second. Every call spends one token.

At time zero the bucket is full, so three calls go straight through. Now it is empty. At half a second, only half a token has refilled, so the next call must wait. At one second there is one whole token, and the call goes.
A semaphore is different. It does not count time, only calls in flight. Limit ten, and the eleventh call waits until one finishes. Use both: rate for the speed, semaphore for the pile.

show.title: Two different caps
items: Token bucket caps calls per second

check.q: A bucket has capacity 3 and rate 1 per second. It is empty now. When can the next call go?
check.why: One token refills each second, and each call spends one, so the next call waits roughly a second.

work: Pick one API client and add a token bucket sized to its published limit.
Add a semaphore to cap in-flight calls so slow responses cannot stack up.

reels.title: Why pipelines run out of memory

beats.say: Why does a pipeline run fine for an hour, then die with an out of memory error?

show.text: Fine for an hour, then out of memory
show.sub: A silent gap between two stages

beats.say: Because the reader is faster than the writer. If the queue between them has no size limit, the gap fills memory. Say the reader makes ten thousand rows a second and the writer takes six thousand. Four thousand extra rows pile up every second.
The fix is a bounded queue, with max size one thousand. When it is full, the reader's put call blocks, so the reader simply sleeps. Slowness travels upstream by itself.

Gotchas. A token bucket without a lock lets two threads spend the same token. Retrying after a four twenty nine with no pause makes things worse, so honour the Retry After header and add random jitter. And a huge bound is no bound at all.

check.q: A reader outpaces a writer through an unbounded queue. What most likely happens?
opts: Memory grows until the process crashes
The queue drops the oldest rows safely
check.why: Without a bound, the surplus accumulates in memory. A bounded queue blocks the reader instead.

work: Replace any unbounded queue in your pipelines with one that has a maxsize.
Make your retry code read Retry After and add jitter.

reels.title: Limiting across many machines

beats.say: Your rate limiter works on one machine. What breaks when you run it on fifty?

show.sub: What is the real limit now?

beats.say: Each machine has its own bucket, so the real limit is fifty times higher. You can split the quota, a fixed share per machine. That is simple, but wastes capacity when load is uneven. Or keep shared counters in Redis. That is accurate, but adds a network hop to every call and a new point of failure.
Decide what happens if Redis is down. Fail open and risk overload, or fail closed and block everyone.
Where possible, prefer pull. A Kafka consumer asks for data when ready, so it needs no limiter at all. Save limiters for the edge, where you cannot control callers.

check.q: You run 50 workers, each with its own bucket at 10 calls per second, against an API limited to 100 per second. What happens?
opts: You can send up to 500 per second and get throttled
check.why: Local buckets are not coordinated, so the total is 50 times 10. Split the quota or share state.

work: Write down the global limit of each dependency and divide it by your worker count.
Decide whether each limiter should fail open or closed, and record why.
Prefer pull-based designs like Kafka consumers where you control both sides.

reels.title: Time it before you fix it

beats.say: Your nightly job takes an hour. Which part is slow? Most people guess, and most people guess wrong.

Picture a restaurant with slow dinners. You blame the chef and hire a second one. Then you time every step with a stopwatch. The chef takes ten minutes. Walking to a faraway storeroom for each ingredient takes forty.
A second chef would have changed nothing. Measuring means timing each step first, so you fix the part that actually hurts.
Then fix in order of biggest win. First a smarter method, like moving the storeroom closer. Then do less work. Adding more cooks comes last.

check.q: Dinners are slow. What should you do first?
opts: Time each step to find the slowest one
check.why: Timing shows where the time really goes. Extra cooks do nothing if the delay is the storeroom walk.

work: Before changing a slow job, write down how long each stage takes.
Ask teammates what they think is slow, then check it with a timer.

reels.title: Profile with cProfile and timeit

beats.say: How do you find the slow line in a Python job without guessing?

Run the job under cProfile, sorted by cumulative time. It lists each function and the total seconds spent inside it, including everything it calls. Read the top twenty lines. Usually one or two functions own most of the time.

To compare two ways of writing one line, use timeit. It repeats the line thousands of times and reports a steady average, so one noisy run cannot fool you. For example, turning a list of a hundred thousand numbers into a set.
The loop is simple. Profile, change one thing, then measure again. If the number did not drop, your guess was wrong.

check.q: Which tool tells you which functions in a whole job use the most time?
check.why: cProfile reports time per function across the run. timeit only benchmarks one small snippet.

work: Profile your slowest pipeline step this week and note the top three functions.
Change one thing at a time and record the before and after time.

reels.title: Fix in order: biggest wins first

beats.say: Why does changing the algorithm beat any amount of tuning?
Say you join ten thousand orders to ten thousand customers with a nested loop. Each order scans every customer. That is one hundred million comparisons.
Instead, build a dictionary of customers by id once. Now each order is one lookup. About twenty thousand steps in total. Thousands of times less work, with no new hardware.
Spark makes the same choice. A nested loop join is the slow scan. A hash or broadcast join is the dictionary. After that come doing less work, vectorised engines, and only last, concurrency.

check.q: A nested loop join over 10,000 by 10,000 rows is slow. Best first fix?
opts: Build a dictionary keyed on the join column
check.why: It cuts about 100 million comparisons to about 20,000 lookups. Threads only split the same huge amount of work.

work: Look for loops inside loops in your code and replace lookups with dicts or sets.
Check Spark plans for nested loop joins and aim for hash or broadcast joins.

reels.title: Why a profile can mislead you

beats.say: Your profile says one function is slow. Why might it still mislead you?
Cumulative time counts everything a function calls, so the top entry is often just the caller. Total time, called tottime, shows time spent in the function itself. Read both columns.

show.title: Two columns
items: Top cumtime is often just main

beats.say: Profiling adds overhead, and tiny test data hides the real hotspot. A join that looks fine on a thousand rows can collapse on a hundred million. Profile with realistic volume.

Micro-benchmarks lie too. Warm caches and tiny inputs flatter code. And a pandas apply with a Python function is still a Python loop, row by row, so it will not speed up like a native column operation.

check.q: Which column shows time spent only in a function's own body?
check.why: tottime excludes callees. cumtime includes them, so it flatters callers like main.

work: Profile with production-sized data, not a ten-row sample.
Read tottime and cumtime together before deciding what to fix.

reels.title: When to stop, and what to choose

beats.say: When a job is slow, should you reach for Spark?
Usually not. Spark adds a cluster, network shuffles, and a lot to operate. A vectorised engine like DuckDB or Polars on one big machine often handles hundreds of gigabytes, faster and cheaper.

Concurrency is the last lever because it adds bugs: races, retries, harder debugging. Threads or asyncio help only when you wait on I/O. Processes help only when you are CPU bound. The profile tells you which.

show.title: Match tool to bottleneck
items: Waiting on I/O: threads or asyncio
Too big for one machine: Spark

beats.say: Also ask if it is worth it. A five minute nightly job nobody waits on may not deserve a week of engineering. Set a target, measure against it, and stop when you reach it.

show.sub: Engineer time costs more than compute

check.q: A job is CPU bound on 200 GB of columnar data. What is the sensible first step after fixing the algorithm?
opts: Try a vectorised engine like DuckDB on one large machine
Move straight to a Spark cluster
check.why: asyncio helps I/O waits, not CPU work. A vectorised engine is cheaper and simpler than a cluster at this size.

work: Write a target runtime before optimising, and stop once you hit it.
Before proposing Spark, test the job in DuckDB or Polars on one large machine.

reels.title: One chopping board: the GIL

beats.say: Why would hiring more cooks sometimes not speed up dinner at all?
Picture a kitchen with only one chopping board. Python has a similar rule called the Global Interpreter Lock, or GIL. Only one thread, a worker inside your program, can run Python code at any moment.
If the job is chopping, extra cooks just queue for the board. But if a cook is waiting for the oven, they step away and hand the board over. Waiting for a website or database works the same way.
So threads help when your program mostly waits, and don't help when it mostly computes.

check.q: A Python script spends most of its time crunching numbers in pure Python. What do extra threads do?
check.why: Only one thread runs Python code at a time because of the GIL, so pure CPU work gains nothing from threads.

work: Before adding threads, ask whether the job mostly waits or mostly computes.
Explain the GIL to a teammate using the one-chopping-board picture.

reels.title: Why threads speed up I/O

beats.say: You run a hundred web requests, one after another, at half a second each. Why can fifty seconds shrink to a few?
A thread that waits on the network releases the GIL. Another thread then runs and sends its own request. With sixteen workers in a thread pool, sixteen requests wait at the same time.

In code, you make a thread pool executor with sixteen workers, and call map with your fetch function over the urls. Results come back in input order. A hundred half-second calls finish in about three to four seconds.

show.title: Thread pool
show.text:
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=16) as pool:
    pages = list(pool.map(fetch, urls))

beats.say: Pure Python math is different. Two threads crunching numbers take as long as one, or longer, because they swap the lock back and forth.

check.q: Why do 16 threads fetch URLs faster than a loop?
opts: Each thread runs Python code on its own core
Waiting threads release the GIL for others
Python turns the GIL off for network code
check.why: While a thread waits on the network it releases the GIL, so many requests wait in parallel even though only one runs Python at a time.

work: Time a loop of 50 HTTP calls against a thread pool of 16 and compare.
Use pool.map when you need results in input order.

reels.title: Races, locks and the GIL's limits

beats.say: If only one thread runs at a time, how can two threads still corrupt a counter?
The GIL can switch threads between bytecode steps. Adding one to a counter is read, add, write. Two threads can both read forty-two, both write forty-three, and one update is lost.
Fix it two ways. Best: give each thread its own data, return a result, and let the main thread merge. Or guard the shared dict with a threading lock, so only one thread touches it at a time.

show.title: Two fixes
items: Each thread returns its own result; main thread merges
Or wrap shared state in a threading Lock

beats.say: Also know this. NumPy, hashing and compression release the GIL, so threads can use many cores there. And since Python 3.14 a free-threaded build with no GIL is officially supported. It is a separate install, and without the GIL, races like this one get more likely, not less.

show.title: Good to know
items: NumPy, hashlib, zlib release the GIL
No GIL means more races, not fewer

check.q: Which design best avoids lost updates across threads?
opts: Rely on the GIL to protect shared dicts
Each thread returns a result; main merges
Add more threads so the updates average out
check.why: The GIL can switch threads mid-update. No shared mutable state means no race; otherwise protect it with a Lock.

work: Review thread code for shared counters or dicts and replace them with returned results.
Where sharing is needed, wrap updates in a threading Lock.

reels.title: Threads, processes or asyncio?

beats.say: Your pipeline is slow. Do you add threads, processes, or something else?

Measure first. If the time is spent waiting on I/O, threads are cheap and share memory, so sixteen to a few dozen workers is a fine start. Beyond that, the remote service's rate limits become the real limit.

If it is pure-Python CPU work, threads give nothing. Use separate processes, which each have their own GIL, but pay for startup and for copying data between them. Or move the hot loop into NumPy or a compiled library.

For thousands of connections, asyncio uses less memory than threads. Free-threaded Python, supported since 3.14, lets threads use every core, but it is a separate build, single-threaded code runs a little slower, and each C library must support it. Benchmark before you bet on it.

show.title: Choosing
items: Check every C library, then benchmark

check.q: A job is CPU-heavy pure Python and runs on 8 cores. What is the best first choice?
opts: A single thread with a Lock
check.why: Each process has its own GIL, so work runs on multiple cores. Threads would still share one GIL.

work: Profile a slow job to see whether it waits or computes before choosing a model.
Check API rate limits before raising thread counts.
Test your key libraries against the free-threaded build before relying on it.
